P/E ratio for PSX stocks explained

The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio compares a company’s share price with its earnings per share. Investors use it as a quick valuation lens. It is useful in context and dangerous in isolation.

By PSX Tracker · Updated 23 September 2026

The basic idea

In simple terms, P/E asks how many years of current earnings you are paying for at today’s price. Providers may use trailing earnings (past periods) or forward estimates (forecasts). Know which one you are reading.

If earnings are near zero or negative, classic P/E can become meaningless or misleading — look at why earnings collapsed before trusting the multiple.

Compare like with like

A bank, a utility and a cyclical manufacturer can deserve different typical ranges. Prefer peers in the same sector and similar business models.

Also compare the same company across years. A multiple that looks “low” versus history may reflect higher risk, not a gift.

Ways P/E fools beginners

  • One-off profits that inflate earnings for a single year
  • Accounting changes that move EPS without changing cash reality
  • Cyclical peaks that make earnings look permanently strong
  • Ignoring debt: two firms with similar P/E can have very different risk

Always open the financial statements behind the ratio.

How this fits portfolio tracking

P/E helps at research time. After you own shares, your personal return is about your cost basis and cashflows. Track those in PSX Tracker; do not confuse the market’s multiple with your performance.

The ratio in one sentence

Price to earnings divides a share price by an earnings-per-share figure. It answers “how many rupees of price am I paying for one rupee of the earnings someone measured?” It does not answer whether the earnings will continue, whether the accounts are aggressive, or whether a peer’s earnings were measured the same way.

You can compute it with last year’s reported earnings, with the last four quarters, or with a forecast. Those are three different ratios. A conversation that does not say which one is a conversation about different numbers. Prefer the one you can recompute from the published accounts, and label a forecast as a forecast.

Earnings per share already spreads profit across the share count. If the company issued shares halfway through the year, the count used in the accounts matters. Read which weighted average they used instead of dividing by today’s share count and calling it close enough.

Why two screens disagree

One source may exclude a one-off gain, a surplus on sale of a plant, or a tax reversal. Another may leave it in. The lower P/E is then an accounting choice, not a cheaper stock. Open the profit note and see how large the unusual item was relative to the profit you are about to divide into.

One source may use the price at the last close. Another may use a price from a different day, or a price adjusted for a bonus the first source has not adjusted. After a bonus or a split, either both the price and the historical earnings per share move together, or neither does. Adjusting only one side invents a cheap or expensive stock.

A loss makes the ratio meaningless or negative. Sorting those names into a “cheap” bucket is a bug in the screener. A tiny profit makes the ratio enormous. Neither extreme is a valuation. It is a sign to read the year instead of the quotient.

Peers, or it is just a number

A P/E of 8 on a cement company and a P/E of 8 on a software exporter are not the same claim. Compare inside an industry, and even then compare the growth, the debt, and the share of earnings that becomes cash. The factors guide is the wider checklist. This page is only the yardstick.

Banks are the classic trap. Earnings can look high because provisions were low, and the more relevant comparison is often price against book value and the return the bank earns on that book. The bank guide covers that. Do not throw bank P/Es into a list with industrial companies and call the sort a research process.

A company that always looks “cheap” on earnings and never converts them to dividends or to a stronger balance sheet may be cheap for a reason you can find in the notes: a regulator, a circular-debt receivable, a sponsor, a plant that needs cash.

What to write down when you use one

Record the price, the date of the price, the period of the earnings, the earnings figure, and the source. “P/E 7” is not reproducible. “Close on this date, earnings for the year ended, page of the annual report” is reproducible. Your future self can then see whether the cheapness was real.

Recompute after the next results. The price will have moved and the earnings will have moved. A thesis that depended on the old ratio needs the new ratio, not loyalty to the old screenshot.

If you cannot explain the earnings in a sentence — what the company sold, and what was unusual — do not use the ratio yet. You would be dividing a price by a number you do not understand, which feels like analysis and is not.

Where this sits in the tracker

Research pages may show a P/E the data vendor computed. Treat it as a clue that points you at the accounts, not as a conclusion. If it disagrees with your arithmetic, your arithmetic from the primary document wins, or you find the definition you missed. Either way you learned something.

The ratio has no place in your cost basis. You do not buy a P/E. You buy shares at a price, plus fees, on a date. The ledger records that. The P/E is a note about whether the price seemed reasonable at the time.

Nothing here says a low ratio is a buy or a high ratio is a sell. Some excellent businesses deserve a higher multiple, and some low multiples are a warning. The accounts tell you which file you are holding.

Common questions

What does a P/E ratio say?

It compares the share price with earnings per share. A low or high number only means something next to peers, growth, and earnings quality.

Why can two P/E ratios disagree?

They may use different earnings periods, share counts, or exclude one-off items. Check which earnings figure the ratio used.

Is a low P/E a bargain?

Not by itself. Earnings can be temporary, falling, or not comparable with another company.
